subject: Geography
name: Geography, Year 10
about: Australian Curriculum, Year 10: Environmental change and management, Geographies of human wellbeing
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Scatter graphs and correlation
points.brief: A scatter graph plots two measures for many places to show whether they rise together, move in opposite directions or show no link. A link does not prove one causes the other.

points.title: Generalisations and predictions
points.brief: A generalisation is a statement that holds for most cases in the data. A prediction extends a trend into the future and is less certain the further ahead it goes.

points.title: Justifying a conclusion
points.brief: A strong conclusion is backed by reliable data from more than one source, and says where the evidence is weak or missing.

points.title: Weighing strategies with criteria
points.brief: To recommend a strategy, compare options against environmental, economic and social criteria, then explain the effects the chosen one is likely to have.

points.title: Environmental functions
points.brief: Environments give resources such as water and timber, absorb wastes, provide services such as clean air and pollination, and hold spiritual meaning.

points.title: Human-induced environmental change
points.brief: People change environments through pollution of air and water, loss of plant and animal species, and degraded land, rivers and seas.

points.title: Conflicting views on sustainability
points.brief: Communities, businesses and governments often disagree about sustainable use, because protecting an environment can cost jobs or profits in the short term.

points.title: Human-centred and earth-centred world views
points.brief: A human-centred world view values nature for what it gives people. An earth-centred world view values nature for its own sake and sees people as part of it.

points.title: How world views shape management
points.brief: People's world views affect whether they see a change as a problem and which ways of managing it they support.

points.title: Custodial responsibility for Country
points.brief: First Nations Australians hold responsibilities to care for Country/Place, passed down through culture and law, which guide how land and water are used.

points.title: Cultural fire management
points.brief: First Nations Australians use cool, small, patchy burns at the right time of year to reduce fuel, protect plants and animals and lower the risk of large bushfires.

points.title: Indigenous rangers
points.brief: Indigenous ranger groups combine cultural knowledge with science to manage Country, such as controlling weeds and feral animals and protecting threatened species.

points.title: Protected areas
points.brief: National parks, marine reserves and World Heritage listing protect environments by limiting what people can do there.

points.title: Spatial strategies
points.brief: Spatial strategies plan where things go, such as wildlife corridors linking patches of bush, or city plans that cut car travel and energy use.

points.title: Trade-offs in environmental decisions
points.brief: Traditional Owners, communities, developers, governments and environment groups weigh environmental, economic and social costs and benefits, and every choice gives something up.

points.title: Comparing management between countries
points.brief: The same problem, such as waste or floods, is managed differently in Australia and other countries, depending on money, technology, laws and values.

points.title: Water use in the Murray-Darling Basin
points.brief: The basin is Australia's largest river system and grows much of its food, so its water is shared between irrigation, towns and the rivers themselves.

points.title: River health in the basin
points.brief: Taking too much water, dams and land clearing have led to salinity, algal blooms, fish kills and drying wetlands.

points.title: The Murray-Darling Basin Plan
points.brief: The Basin Plan sets limits on how much water can be taken and returns some to the rivers as environmental flows, which divides farmers, towns and conservationists.

points.title: First Nations voices on water
points.brief: First Nations peoples of the basin seek cultural flows, water they own and manage to care for Country and support their communities.

points.title: Human wellbeing and development
points.brief: Human wellbeing is the quality of people's lives, including health, education, income, safety and freedom. Development is the process of improving it.

points.title: GDP per person
points.brief: Gross domestic product per person shows a country's average income, but it says nothing about how fairly income is shared or about health and education.

points.title: The Human Development Index
points.brief: The HDI combines life expectancy, years of schooling and income per person into a score from 0 to 1, so countries can be ranked on more than income.

points.title: Other wellbeing measures
points.brief: Measures such as the Multidimensional Poverty Index count what people lack, such as clean water, schooling or electricity, to show poverty that income alone misses.

points.title: The Sustainable Development Goals
points.brief: The United Nations set 17 goals for 2030, such as ending poverty and hunger and good health and education, which countries track to improve wellbeing.

points.title: Causes of wellbeing differences
points.brief: Wellbeing differs between and within countries because of resources, health and education services, jobs and income, technology and government.

points.title: Wellbeing within India
points.brief: Wellbeing in India varies widely, with higher incomes and services in cities such as Mumbai than in poorer rural areas of states such as Rajasthan.

points.title: Urban and remote Australia
points.brief: People in remote Australia often have lower incomes, fewer services and shorter lives on average than people in the major cities.

points.title: First Nations wellbeing and Closing the Gap
points.brief: Gaps remain between First Nations and other Australians in health, education and jobs. Closing the Gap sets shared targets, with First Nations communities as partners.

points.title: Reducing regional inequality
points.brief: Governments run programs to lift wellbeing in poorer regions, such as building roads, clinics and schools in rural Papua New Guinea or Indonesia.

points.title: Australian overseas aid
points.brief: The Australian Government gives aid to countries in Asia and the Pacific for health, education, infrastructure and disaster recovery.

points.title: Non-government organisations
points.brief: Non-government organisations such as World Vision raise money and run programs, such as clean water and schooling, to improve wellbeing.

points.title: Community-led change in remote communities
points.brief: Programs work best in remote First Nations communities when the communities lead them, such as locally run health services and ranger jobs.
